simple: a piece of Verilog that runs again whenever something it waits for happens.
analogy: a standing instruction: "whenever the bell rings, do this".
precise: a procedural block with an event control; always @(posedge clk) describes edge-triggered storage, always @(*) describes combinational logic.
source: D6 “always Statement”, “Combinational Logic using always” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the wire that carries one bit into or out of the selected cell.
analogy: the hatch through which a jar's level is passed out.
precise: a column line shared by all cells in a column; SRAM uses a pair (bit line and its complement), DRAM one line per cell column.
source: D5 6T cell, D6 §2.2 of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the file that tells the FPGA what to become.
analogy: the full setup sheet for the hall: every answer card and every cable.
precise: the configuration data, produced by the vendor toolchain, that sets every LUT, flip-flop option and routing switch of a specific device.
source: D6 ch. 1 of F1-22 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: ready-made memory blocks inside the FPGA.
analogy: built-in pantry shelves in the hall.
precise: dedicated SRAM blocks in the FPGA fabric, usually with synchronous (clocked) read ports.
source: D8 RAMB18E1 of F1-22 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: =: the new value is used by the very next line.
analogy: passing a plate hand to hand along a line of cooks in one go.
precise: a procedural assignment that completes before the next statement executes; the right style for combinational always @(*) blocks.
source: D6 “Blocking vs. Nonblocking Assignment” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the moment a clock signal changes, from 0 to 1 (rising) or from 1 to 0 (falling).
analogy: the instant the bell rings, not the time between rings.
precise: a transition of the clock signal; a rising-edge-triggered flip-flop samples its input at the 0-to-1 transition. Clocks themselves are the subject of F1-18.
source: D6 “D Flip-Flop” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a signal that tells flip-flops "this edge counts" or "skip this edge".
analogy: a card held up at some rings that says "the dessert station works on this ring only".
precise: a control input that makes clocked elements update only on edges where it is 1, so slow parts of a design can share the main clock.
source: D5 §2.2.3.6 of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: how many clock cycles happen in one second.
analogy: rings per second.
precise: f = 1 / T, measured in hertz (Hz, cycles per second); 1 MHz is 10^6 Hz and 1 GHz is 10^9 Hz.
source: W1 of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the time from one rising edge to the next.
analogy: the time between two rings of the bell.
precise: the duration T of one cycle of the clock, measured in seconds (often ns).
source: D3 “Setup Time Constraint”, W1 of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a signal that goes 0, 1, 0, 1 at a steady beat and tells flip-flops when to store.
analogy: the pass bell, rung at a steady beat.
precise: a periodic digital signal whose edges (here the rising edges) trigger the flip-flops of a synchronous circuit.
source: D3 “Synchronous Sequential Logic” of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the clock edge reaching different flip-flops at slightly different times.
analogy: cooks far from the bell hear the ring a little later.
precise: the difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at two clocked elements, caused by the clock distribution wiring.
source: D3 “Clock Skew” of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: how long a flip-flop takes to show its new value after the edge.
analogy: the moment a cook needs to pick up the handed-over dish.
precise: the delay from the active clock edge to the flip-flop's output Q becoming valid.
source: D3 “Timing” of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a circuit whose outputs depend only on its inputs right now.
analogy: a cook who answers "what goes with fish?" the same way every time, with no notebook.
precise: a circuit without memory: after the propagation delay, its outputs are a fixed function of its current inputs (the gates, adders and multiplexers of HW102).
source: D2 §3.1 of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: one repeated tile of the FPGA, with lookup tables and flip-flops.
analogy: one movable station.
precise: the basic logic tile of an FPGA, usually grouping LUTs, flip-flops, multiplexers and carry logic; names and contents differ by vendor.
source: D7 “CLB Overview”, D5 “LE: Logic Element” of F1-22 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a file that says which pin is which and how fast the clock is.
analogy: the list of which hall door is the delivery door.
precise: a toolchain input mapping top-level ports to package pins and stating clock periods and I/O standards; its format is vendor-specific.
source: F1-22 (not verified against a vendor manual: see the unverified box in F1-22, Layer 3)

simple: a register that adds 1 to itself at each clock edge.
analogy: the "take a number" display at the door.
precise: a sequential circuit whose state steps through a fixed sequence, usually binary 0, 1, 2, ..., 2^n − 1 and then wraps to 0.
source: D7 “Counters” of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the slowest route signals must travel before the result is ready.
analogy: the soup station: the longest job between two rings.
precise: the path between two clocked elements with the longest total delay; it sets the minimum clock period (see also F1-15 and HW202).
source: D3 “Setup Time Constraint” of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a latch with one data input D and one enable input.
analogy: the serving hatch with one plate slot.
precise: a latch whose output Q follows D while the enable input is 1 and holds its last value while the enable input is 0; it avoids the forbidden input of the SR latch.
source: D6 “D Latch” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: memory that stores each bit as a tiny electric charge, which leaks away and must be topped up.
analogy: the evaporating jars.
precise: random-access memory whose cell is one access transistor and one capacitor; the charge leaks, so the cells must be refreshed periodically, and reading disturbs the charge, so a read must be followed by a write-back.
source: D6 §2.2, §2.4, D4 “DRAM” of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the share of each period in which the clock is 1.
analogy: how long the bell's hammer stays up compared with the whole beat.
precise: high time divided by period, written as a percentage; the clocks in this chapter's simulations are 50 % (equal high and low halves).
source: W1 of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: an output wired back to an input of the same circuit.
analogy: two cooks who each keep repeating what the other one said a moment ago.
precise: a connection that forms a loop from a gate's output back to its own input, directly or through other gates; feedback is what lets a circuit hold a value. (The robotics and control courses use "feedback" for a different idea: measuring a result and correcting towards a target.)
source: D6 “Bistable Circuit” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a circuit that is always in one of a few named situations and moves between them by rules.
analogy: the order's status card and Rosa's rule card.
precise: a sequential circuit with a finite set of states, a state register holding the current state, next-state logic that computes the next state from the current state and inputs, and output logic.
source: D5 “Finite State Machines (FSMs)” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a one-bit memory that changes only at one instant: the clock's edge.
analogy: a ticket clip on the rail that may be swapped only when the bell rings.
precise: an edge-triggered storage element; a D flip-flop copies D to Q at the active edge of its clock (here the rising edge) and holds Q at all other times.
source: D6 “D Flip-Flop”, D2 §3.2.1 of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a chip whose circuit you can choose, and change, after it is made.
analogy: the event-hall kitchen of movable stations.
precise: an integrated circuit made of an array of configurable logic blocks, programmable interconnect and I/O blocks, whose function is set by loading configuration data.
source: D5 “FPGAs: Field Programmable Gate Arrays”, “General FPGA Layout”, D6 ch. 1 of F1-22 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a short wrong value that appears while signals are changing.
analogy: the display flashing a wrong number for a blink before it settles.
precise: a brief unintended value on a signal, caused by inputs or bits that change at slightly different times.
source: D8 Description of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a text language for describing circuits.
analogy: the floor plan, written in words.
precise: a language such as Verilog or VHDL whose descriptions can be simulated and synthesised into hardware; most statements describe hardware that runs concurrently.
source: D6 “HDL: Hardware Description Language”, “HDL Simulation”, “HDL Synthesis” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: how long after the edge the input must stay steady.
analogy: nobody may snatch the dish off the pass in the instant of the ring.
precise: the minimum time after the active clock edge during which D must remain stable.
source: D3 “Timing”, D7 Timing requirements of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a bit pattern in the state register that is not one of your states.
analogy: a status card with a word that is not on the rule card.
precise: a code the state register can hold but the design never meant to use; robust designs define a safe next state for it.
source: D6 “Combinational Logic using case” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a latch you did not ask for, created because your description forgot a case.
analogy: a cook who, when an order is missing, keeps serving the previous one.
precise: a latch that a synthesis tool creates from a hardware description in which some output is not assigned on every path through the logic, so the description implies "keep the old value".
source: D7 “Latch”, D5 proc_dlatch, R3 of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a one-bit memory that can change whenever its control input says "open".
analogy: the serving hatch: while it is open, the newest plate is what you see; when it closes, the last plate stays in view.
precise: a level-sensitive storage element: while its enable (or clock) input is at the active level the output follows the data input ("transparent"); otherwise the output holds.
source: D6 “D Latch” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a program that reads code and points out suspicious lines.
analogy: an inspector who reads the floor plan before anything is built.
precise: a static checker that reports problems such as width mismatches, unused signals and inferred latches without simulating.
source: D4, R4, R7 of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the input that says "store the new value at the next edge".
analogy: the cook's nod that says "yes, swap my ticket at this ring".
precise: a control input of a register: at a clock edge, if load = 1 the register takes its data input, otherwise it keeps its value.
source: D5 “Enabled Flip-Flops” of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a tiny memory that stores the answer for every input pattern.
analogy: the station's answer card: find your inputs' line and read the answer.
precise: a k-input LUT is a 2^k-bit memory addressed by its k inputs; its contents are configuration bits, so it implements any Boolean function of k inputs.
source: D7 “Look-Up Table”, D5 “LE: Logic Element” of F1-22 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a state machine whose outputs also look at the inputs right now.
analogy: a waiter who reacts to the status card and to the customer's wave at the same time.
precise: an FSM whose outputs are a function of the current state and the current inputs; it can respond in the same cycle, at the cost of outputs that follow input changes between edges.
source: D5 “Mealy FSM Example” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: cells arranged in rows and columns.
analogy: the pantry shelves.
precise: a two-dimensional grid of cells with a row decoder driving word lines and column circuits on the bit lines.
source: D4 “Memory Arrays”, D5 row decoder, column circuitry of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the smallest part of a memory: it stores one bit.
analogy: one flip sign, or one jar.
precise: a circuit storing one bit that can be selected for reading and writing by a word line and connected to one or two bit lines.
source: D4 “Memory Array Bit Cells”, D5 6T cell of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a storage element caught exactly halfway between 0 and 1 for a while.
analogy: a coin that lands on its edge and wobbles before it falls.
precise: a state in which a bistable element's output lingers between the two valid levels for an unpredictable time, caused by inputs that change too close to the sampling instant or by S and R released together.
source: D6 “Metastability” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: one named block of hardware with inputs and outputs.
analogy: one station on the floor plan, with its doors.
precise: the Verilog unit of design: a port list, declarations and statements; modules are instantiated inside other modules to build a hierarchy.
source: D6 “SystemVerilog Modules”, “Module Declaration” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a state machine whose outputs depend only on the state.
analogy: the waiters look only at the status card, not at what Rosa is hearing.
precise: an FSM whose outputs are a function of the current state alone; outputs change only after a clock edge.
source: D5 “Finite State Machines (FSMs)” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the part that decides where to go next.
analogy: Rosa reading her rule card.
precise: combinational logic computing the next state from the current state and the inputs; it is stored into the state register at the clock edge.
source: D5 “Finite State Machines (FSMs)” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: <=: every right-hand side is read first, and all the left-hand sides change together afterwards.
analogy: at the bell, every cook hands their plate to the next station at the same moment.
precise: a procedural assignment whose update is scheduled after all right-hand sides in the time step are evaluated; the right style for clocked always @(posedge clk) blocks, matching the behaviour of flip-flops.
source: D6 “Blocking vs. Nonblocking Assignment”, “Rules for Signal Assignment” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the part that makes the clock's steady beat in the first place.
analogy: Rosa's metronome.
precise: a circuit that produces a periodic signal; digital systems derive their clocks from one, often multiplied or divided on the chip.
source: D5 §2.2.3 of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a named number you can change when you use the module.
analogy: "this counter is N metres long" on the plan.
precise: a module constant, such as a width, that each instance can override.
source: D6 “Parameterized Module” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: deciding which block does which job and which wires connect them.
analogy: deciding where each station stands and which cables to run.
precise: the tool steps that assign netlist cells to physical sites on the device and choose routing resources, followed by timing analysis.
source: D5 “FPGA Design Flow”, D11 §2 of F1-22 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a named connection into or out of a module.
analogy: a door of the station.
precise: a module's interface signal, declared input, output or inout with a width.
source: D6 “Module Declaration” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: wires with switches that can be set to connect any block to others.
analogy: the floor sockets and cables between stations.
precise: routing channels and switch boxes whose connections are set by configuration bits.
source: D5 “FPGAs: Field Programmable Gate Arrays”, D6 ch. 1 of F1-22 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: reading each row and writing it back before its charge leaks too far.
analogy: Sam topping up the jars, row by row.
precise: periodic read-and-restore of every DRAM row within a maximum interval set by the part's specification.
source: D6 §2.4 of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a row of flip-flops that store one number together.
analogy: a row of ticket clips on the rail, all swapped at the same ring of the bell.
precise: n D flip-flops sharing one clock, storing an n-bit value; extra inputs (load or enable, reset) decide whether a clock edge stores new data, clears, or keeps the value. The CPU registers named by instructions (HW202, "Register (CPU)") are built this way.
source: D5 “Registers”, D2 §3.2.2 of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the input that clears a register to a known value, usually 0.
analogy: wiping the rail clean before service.
precise: a synchronous reset acts only at a clock edge; an asynchronous reset acts at once, without waiting for the clock.
source: D5 “Resettable Flip-Flops”, D8 Description of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a counter in which each bit's change triggers the next bit, one after another.
analogy: a line of cooks who each start only when the neighbour has finished.
precise: a counter in which only the lowest flip-flop is clocked by the clock and each other flip-flop is clocked by the output of the one before it; the bits change at different times.
source: D9 §1, §4, D11 §1.2.2.3 of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a circuit that notices a very small change on a bit line and turns it into a clear 0 or 1.
analogy: Sam's practised eye for "more or less than half full".
precise: a differential amplifier on each bit line that resolves the small voltage change caused by a cell into a full logic level (and, in DRAM, restores the cell).
source: D5 sense amplifiers, D6 §2.2 of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a circuit whose outputs also depend on what happened before.
analogy: a kitchen with a ticket rail: what it cooks next depends on the tickets already clipped there.
precise: a circuit with memory: its outputs depend on its current inputs and on its stored state, which records information about past inputs.
source: D6 “Sequential Circuits” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: how long before the edge a flip-flop's input must already be steady.
analogy: the dish must be on the pass a moment before the ring, not during it.
precise: the minimum time before the active clock edge during which D must be stable for the flip-flop to sample it reliably.
source: D3 “Timing”, D7 Timing requirements of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a register whose bits move one place at each clock edge.
analogy: the plate conveyor on the pass.
precise: a chain of flip-flops in which each flip-flop's input is the previous one's output; a serial input enters at one end at each edge.
source: D7 “Shift Registers”, D10 §1 of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: how much time is left over in a clock period after the slowest work is done.
analogy: the seconds the soup cook can rest before the ring.
precise: clock period minus the time the path needs; negative slack means the path fails timing.
source: D6 §2.2.2, W1 of F1-18 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a latch with a Set button and a Reset button.
analogy: a "table taken" sign with two levers: one flips it to taken, the other to free.
precise: a latch made of two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates, with inputs S (set, makes Q = 1) and R (reset, makes Q = 0); S = R = 1 is not allowed.
source: D6 “SR Latch” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: memory whose cells hold their bit for as long as the power is on.
analogy: the flip signs.
precise: random-access memory whose cell is a bistable loop of two cross-coupled inverters plus access transistors (six transistors in the common design); "static" means no refresh is needed.
source: D5 6T cell, D4 “SRAM” of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the situation the machine is in right now.
analogy: the word on the status card.
precise: the value held in the state register; it summarises everything about past inputs that the machine needs for its future behaviour.
source: D5 “Finite State Machine (FSM)” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a drawing with a circle for each state and an arrow for each move.
analogy: the flow chart pinned beside the order board.
precise: a directed graph whose nodes are states and whose edges are transitions, labelled with the input conditions that cause them (and, for Mealy machines, the outputs).
source: D5 “Moore FSM Example”, “Mealy FSM Example” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the bit pattern chosen for each state.
analogy: a numbered status card instead of a word.
precise: an assignment of binary codes to states; binary encoding uses ⌈log₂(number of states)⌉ flip-flops, one-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state.
source: D5 state-encoding slides, W1 of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the same information as the diagram, written as a table.
analogy: Rosa's rule card.
precise: a table listing, for each current state and input combination, the next state (and outputs).
source: D5 “FSM Design Procedure” of F1-19 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a counter in which all bits change at the same clock edge.
analogy: all digits of the display flip at the same ring.
precise: a counter whose flip-flops share one clock; the next value is computed by combinational logic (an incrementer) from the current value.
source: D8 Description, D2 §3.2.4 of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a program that turns HDL into a list of gates and flip-flops.
analogy: the builder turning the plan into real stations.
precise: a tool that maps a synthesisable HDL description to a netlist of cells of a target technology.
source: D6 “HDL Synthesis”, D5 synth of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the parts of the language that can become real hardware.
analogy: plan notes a builder can build; "paint it later" is not one.
precise: the constructs a synthesis tool accepts; delays such as #5, $display and most initial blocks are for simulation only.
source: D6 “Testbenches” of F1-21 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a picture of signals as lines that go up and down over time.
analogy: a strip showing, minute by minute, which tickets were on the rail.
precise: a plot of signal values (horizontal axis: time) used to show the order of events; in this course they are drawn from real simulation runs.
source: D6 “D Latch vs. D Flip-Flop” of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the simulator's way of saying "this could be 0 or 1; I cannot tell".
analogy: a ticket clip before anyone has clipped a ticket.
precise: in Verilog simulation a 1-bit signal has four values: 0, 1, x (unknown) and z (not driven); storage starts as x until something sets it.
source: D7 “Z: Floating Output”, R1 of F1-16 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: memory that forgets when the power goes off.
analogy: the signs fall when the lights go out; the jars dry out.
precise: memory that loses its contents without power; SRAM and DRAM are both volatile.
source: D5 memory taxonomy of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: the wire that picks one row of cells.
analogy: the shelf label Sam reads to pick a row.
precise: the row-select line, driven by the address decoder, that turns on the access transistors of every cell in one row.
source: D6 §2.2, D5 row decoder of F1-20 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: after the biggest number, the counter goes back to 0.
analogy: the display after 99 shows 00.
precise: arithmetic modulo 2^n: in 4 bits, 15 + 1 = 0 (see MA102).
source: W1 of F1-17 (checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a list of the parts of a circuit and the wires that connect them.
analogy: the builder's parts list for the kitchen, with every cable between the stations.
precise: a description of a circuit as instances of cells (gates, flip-flops, lookup tables) and the nets connecting them; the output of a synthesis tool.
source: D5 of F1-21 (see that chapter's Sources; re-checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)

simple: a program that pretends to be a circuit, and a piece of code that tries it out and checks the answers.
analogy: a rehearsal of the kitchen on paper, and the head chef's checklist used during it.
precise: a logic simulator computes signal values over time from an HDL description; a testbench is simulation-only HDL code that drives a design's inputs and checks its outputs, ideally printing a pass or fail verdict itself.
source: D1 of F1-16 (see that chapter's Sources; re-checked in the verification pass, 2026-10-10)
